Which nodes matter most? The question sounds simple, but "matter" can mean many things: having the
most connections, being close to everyone else, sitting on the routes between others, or being
connected to other important nodes. Each meaning leads to a different *centrality measure*, and
EdgeCase implements several dozen of them. This page explains the main families, shows how to
compute and compare them, and points out the cases where the choice of measure changes the answer.

The main families, and the methods that implement them, are these:

| Family | Asks | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| Degree | How many neighbors does a node have? | [`degree_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.degree_centrality.qmd) |
| Distance | How close is a node to all the others? | [`closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.closeness_centrality.qmd), [`harmonic_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.harmonic_centrality.qmd), [`current_flow_closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.current_flow_closeness_centrality.qmd) |
| Betweenness | How often does a node lie on the routes between others? | [`betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.betweenness_centrality.qmd), [`edge_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.edge_betweenness_centrality.qmd), [`load_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.load_centrality.qmd), [`current_flow_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.current_flow_betweenness_centrality.qmd) |
| Spectral | Is a node connected to other central nodes? | [`eigen_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.eigen_centrality.qmd), [`katz_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.katz_centrality.qmd), [`pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.pagerank.qmd), [`personalized_pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.personalized_pagerank.qmd) |
| Hubs and authorities | Does a node point to good sources, or is it pointed to by good hubs? | [`hub_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.hub_centrality.qmd), [`authority_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.authority_centrality.qmd) |
| Brokerage | Does a node bridge otherwise separate contacts? | [`constraint()`](../reference/Graph.constraint.qmd), [`effective_size()`](../reference/Graph.effective_size.qmd) |
| Spreading | Which nodes would spread something furthest? | [`voterank()`](../reference/Graph.voterank.qmd), [`percolation_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.percolation_centrality.qmd) |

## How the centrality methods work

Every centrality method that scores the nodes follows the convention set out in
[Get started](get-started.qmd#three-ideas-that-run-through-the-library). It stores the scores in
a node attribute named after the method, and returns the graph so that calls can be chained:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.betweenness_centrality()
karate.get_node_df().select("id", "label", "faction", "betweenness_centrality").head(3)
```

Two arguments, accepted by all of them, change this. `attr_name=` stores the scores under another
name, which is how to keep two variants of the same measure side by side, and `return_dict=True`
returns the scores as a dictionary keyed by node ID, leaving the graph unchanged:

```{python}
scores = karate.closeness_centrality(return_dict=True)
round(scores[1], 3)
```

Because the scores are stored as columns of the node table, Polars is the natural tool for ranking
and comparing them. Computing seven measures in one chain and sorting by one of them gives a
first look at the club's most central members:

```{python}
measures = [
    "degree_centrality",
    "closeness_centrality",
    "harmonic_centrality",
    "betweenness_centrality",
    "eigen_centrality",
    "pagerank",
    "katz_centrality",
]

(
    karate
    .degree_centrality()
    .closeness_centrality()
    .harmonic_centrality()
    .eigen_centrality()
    .pagerank()
    .katz_centrality()
)

karate.get_node_df().select("label", *measures).sort("pagerank", descending=True)
```

The instructor (label `"0"`) and the administrator (label `"33"`) lead on nearly every measure, as
the two people the club eventually split around. Below them, the measures begin to disagree, and
the rest of this page explains why.

## Degree centrality

The simplest measure is a node's degree. [`degree_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.degree_centrality.qmd)
divides it by `n - 1`, the largest degree possible, so that the score is the fraction of the other
nodes that a node is linked to:

```{python}
karate.get_degree(1), round(karate.get_node(1).attributes["degree_centrality"], 3)
```

The instructor has 16 friends among the 33 other members, a degree centrality of 0.485. In a
directed graph, `mode=` chooses what to count: `"in"` for incoming edges, `"out"` for outgoing
ones, and `"all"` (the default) for both. Use `attr_name=` to keep the variants apart, as in
`degree_centrality(mode="in", attr_name="in_degree")`.

Degree is cheap to compute and often a good first approximation, but it is purely local. A node
with many neighbors in a remote corner of the network scores as highly as a node with the same
number of neighbors at its heart.

## Closeness and harmonic centrality

The distance family scores a node by how near it is to everyone else.
[`closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.closeness_centrality.qmd) is the reciprocal of the
mean distance from a node to the others, so a node that is one step from everyone scores 1. The
instructor is again the most central member of the club, but the administrator's lieutenant (ID 3,
label `"2"`) comes second, ahead of the administrator. They have only ten friends, but those friends
are spread across both factions:

```{python}
(
    karate.get_node_df()
    .select("id", "label", "degree", "closeness_centrality")
    .sort("closeness_centrality", descending=True)
    .head(5)
)
```

Closeness has a well-known weakness: in a disconnected graph, some distances are infinite. EdgeCase
follows the usual remedy, computing each node's closeness over the nodes it can reach and then
scaling it by the fraction of the graph that is. This correction, due to Wasserman and Faust, is
on by default and controlled by `wf_improved=`. Its effect is easiest to see on a graph of two
separate paths, one of four nodes and one of two:

```{python}
two_paths = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=4).add_path_graph(n=2)
(
    two_paths.closeness_centrality(return_dict=True),
    two_paths.closeness_centrality(wf_improved=False, return_dict=True),
)
```

Without the correction, the two nodes of the short path (IDs 5 and 6) score a perfect 1, since each
is one step from everything *it can reach*. With it, they score lowest, since they can reach only
one of the five other nodes.

[`harmonic_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.harmonic_centrality.qmd) avoids the problem
altogether by summing the *reciprocals* of the distances, so that an unreachable node simply
contributes 0. Its raw value is a sum rather than an average, and `normalized=True` divides it by
`n - 1` to give a score between 0 and 1:

```{python}
harmonic = karate.harmonic_centrality(normalized=True, return_dict=True)
round(karate.get_node(1).attributes["harmonic_centrality"], 2), round(harmonic[1], 3)
```

Both measures accept `mode=` for directed graphs (`"out"` measures distances from a node, `"in"`
distances to it) and `weighted=` for weighted graphs, in which distances are total edge weights.
[`current_flow_closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.current_flow_closeness_centrality.qmd),
also called information centrality, is a variant that treats the graph as an electrical network,
and so counts every path between two nodes rather than only the shortest.

## Betweenness centrality

[`betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.betweenness_centrality.qmd) measures how often a
node lies on the shortest paths between other nodes. A node with high betweenness controls the
flow of whatever travels along shortest paths, whether information, goods, or influence, and its
removal lengthens many routes. The scores are normalized to lie between 0 and 1, where 1 would mean
that a node lies on every shortest path between every other pair.

The classic illustration is the marriage network of Renaissance Florence. The Medici were not the
wealthiest family, nor the best connected by marriage, yet they came to dominate the city.
Betweenness suggests why:

```{python}
florentine = ec.florentine_families().degrees().betweenness_centrality()
(
    florentine.get_node_df()
    .select("label", "degree", "betweenness_centrality")
    .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True)
    .head(6)
)
```

The Medici lie on more than half of all the shortest paths between other families, twice the share
of the next family. Their six marriages linked families that were otherwise poorly connected to one
another, which made the Medici the indispensable intermediaries of Florentine politics. The
Salviati, with only two marriages, rank fourth: they are the only link between the Pazzi and the
rest of the network.

### Weighted betweenness

On a weighted graph, betweenness follows the weighted shortest paths, which treat each weight as a
*length*. That is right for distances and travel times, but many networks have weights that
measure the *strength* of a tie, such as the number of messages exchanged or the number of
meetings. A shortest path that prefers weak ties makes little sense for those.

The Les Misérables network is an example. Its weights count the chapters in which two characters
appear together, so a high weight means a close relationship:

```{python}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()

def top_five(graph, scores):
    ranked = sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
    return [graph.get_label_from_id(node) for node in ranked[:5]]

top_five(miserables, miserables.betweenness_centrality(return_dict=True))
```

Taken as lengths, the co-occurrence counts route shortest paths through the characters who share
few scenes. The usual remedy is to invert the weights, so that strong ties become short:

```{python}
miserables.set_edge_attrs(
    "weight",
    {edge["id"]: 1 / edge["weight"] for edge in miserables.get_edge_df().iter_rows(named=True)},
)
top_five(miserables, miserables.betweenness_centrality(return_dict=True))
```

Valjean still comes first, but Marius, Fantine, and the student Courfeyrac, whose strong ties bind
the novel's storylines together, now replace Gavroche, Javert, and Thénardier. For comparison,
`weighted=False` ignores the weights altogether. Whichever choice you make, make it deliberately:
EdgeCase can't tell whether a weight is a length or a strength.

### Edge betweenness

[`edge_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.edge_betweenness_centrality.qmd) applies the
same idea to edges, and stores its scores as an edge attribute. Edges with high betweenness are the
bridges between groups, which is why repeatedly removing them is one way of finding communities
(see [Communities](communities.qmd)). In the karate club, the edge with the highest betweenness
joins the instructor to member `"31"`, who belongs to the other faction:

```{python}
karate.edge_betweenness_centrality()
top_edge = karate.get_edge_df().sort("edge_betweenness_centrality", descending=True).row(0, named=True)
[
    (karate.get_label_from_id(top_edge[end]), karate.get_node(top_edge[end]).attributes["faction"])
    for end in ("source", "target")
]
```

Only ten friendships cross between the factions, and many of the shortest paths from the
instructor's circle to the members around `"31"` run along this one, so it carries more traffic
than any other edge.

### Variants

Several variants of betweenness change what counts as a route:

| Method | Counts |
|---|---|
| [`load_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.load_centrality.qmd) | flow split equally at each branch of the shortest paths, rather than across them |
| [`current_flow_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.current_flow_betweenness_centrality.qmd) | every path, weighted as current in an electrical network (also called random-walk betweenness) |
| [`approximate_current_flow_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.approximate_current_flow_betweenness_centrality.qmd) | the same, estimated from a sample of pairs |
| [`communicability_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.communicability_betweenness_centrality.qmd) | walks of every length, with longer walks counting for less |
| [`betweenness_centrality_subset()`](../reference/Graph.betweenness_centrality_subset.qmd) | only the paths from given sources to given targets |
| [`edge_load_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.edge_load_centrality.qmd), [`edge_current_flow_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.edge_current_flow_betweenness_centrality.qmd) | edge versions of load and current-flow betweenness |

### Groups of nodes

Sometimes the question is about a set of nodes rather than one: what share of the network's
traffic would a team of monitors see between them?
[`group_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.group_betweenness_centrality.qmd) answers it
for a group you choose, counting the shortest paths that pass through *at least one* member:

```{python}
round(karate.group_betweenness_centrality([1, 34]), 3)
```

The instructor and the administrator together lie on about 69% of the shortest paths between the
other members. [`prominent_group()`](../reference/Graph.prominent_group.qmd) searches for the best
group of a given size, and returns its score and members:

```{python}
karate.prominent_group(3)
```

Adding member `"32"` (ID 33) raises the share to 81%. The best group of `k` isn't always the `k`
individually most central nodes, since two nodes on the same routes see the same traffic; on large
graphs, `greedy=True` trades optimality for speed.
[`group_closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.group_closeness_centrality.qmd) and
[`group_degree_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.group_degree_centrality.qmd) are the closeness and
degree equivalents.

## Spectral centrality

The spectral measures rest on a recursive idea: a node is important if it is linked to other
important nodes. Solving that circular definition requires the eigenvectors of the adjacency
matrix, from which the family takes its name.

[`eigen_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.eigen_centrality.qmd) applies the idea directly: each
node's score is proportional to the sum of its neighbors' scores. It rewards a node for being
connected to the well-connected, so in the karate club it ranks the administrator first, since
their friends include the members with the most friends. One point to note for directed graphs:
EdgeCase sums the scores of a node's *successors*, so a node is central if it points to central
nodes. NetworkX sums those of its predecessors instead.

[`katz_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.katz_centrality.qmd) adds a baseline score, `beta=`, to
every node, so that nodes with no central neighbors, and nodes in directed graphs that nothing
points to, still receive credit. Its `alpha=` sets how quickly the influence of distant nodes
fades. The calculation only converges when `alpha` is below the reciprocal of the adjacency
matrix's largest eigenvalue (about 0.149 for the karate club), and EdgeCase emits a
`RuntimeWarning` when it isn't. The default of 0.1 is safe for most sparse networks, but dense
graphs may need a smaller value. [`alpha_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.alpha_centrality.qmd)
and [`bonacich_power_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.bonacich_power_centrality.qmd) are close
relatives.

### PageRank

[`pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.pagerank.qmd) is the measure Google used to rank web pages. It
models a reader who follows links at random and, with probability `1 - damping` at each step,
jumps to a random page instead. A node's PageRank is the fraction of time the reader spends there,
so the scores sum to 1. The random jumps make PageRank well defined on any directed graph, even
one with nodes that have no outgoing links.

PageRank is most interesting in directed networks, where it differs most from simply counting
incoming links. In Wikipedia's administrator elections, an edge from one user to another is a vote:

```{python}
votes = ec.wiki_vote().pagerank().degree_centrality(mode="in", attr_name="in_degree")
(
    votes.get_node_df()
    .select("label", "pagerank", "in_degree")
    .sort("pagerank", descending=True)
    .head(5)
)
```

The top two users are also the two who received the most votes. User `"6633"` is different: they
rank third by PageRank with less than half the votes of the leader, because their votes came from
users who themselves received many votes. In-degree counts the votes; PageRank also weighs them.

[`personalized_pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.personalized_pagerank.qmd) makes every random jump
land on a chosen set of nodes, given as a dictionary of node IDs and weights. The result measures
importance *from the point of view of* those nodes, which makes it useful for recommendations and
for finding the nodes most relevant to a seed. From member `"11"` (ID 12), whose only friend is the
instructor, the instructor's circle dominates:

```{python}
personal = karate.personalized_pagerank({12: 1.0}, return_dict=True)
[(node, round(score, 3)) for node, score in sorted(personal.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:5]]
```

The instructor scores even higher than member `"11"` themselves. The administrator (ID 34), who
leads the club-wide ranking, comes fifth.

## Hubs and authorities

Kleinberg's HITS algorithm gives each node of a directed graph two scores. A good *authority* is
pointed to by many good hubs, and a good *hub* points to many good authorities.
[`authority_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.authority_centrality.qmd) and
[`hub_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.hub_centrality.qmd) compute the two scores, and the
distinction suits the election network well: authorities are the candidates whom respected voters
supported, and hubs are the voters who supported respected candidates.

```{python}
votes.hub_centrality().authority_centrality()
(
    votes.get_node_df()
    .select("label", "hub_centrality", "authority_centrality")
    .sort("hub_centrality", descending=True)
    .head(3)
)
```

The leading hubs have authority scores of zero: they cast many votes for successful candidates but
received none themselves. In an undirected graph, hubs and authorities coincide, and both equal
eigenvector centrality.

## Brokerage

Ronald Burt's theory of *structural holes* holds that a person whose contacts don't know one
another is well placed to broker between them, and to learn things the others don't. Two measures
capture this.

[`constraint()`](../reference/Graph.constraint.qmd) measures how much a node's contacts are
connected to one another, and so how little room they leave it to broker. Lower values mean more
brokerage opportunity. [`effective_size()`](../reference/Graph.effective_size.qmd) counts a node's
contacts, discounted for the ties among them, so a node whose contacts are all strangers to one
another has an effective size equal to its degree.

```{python}
karate.constraint().effective_size()
(
    karate.get_node_df()
    .select("id", "label", "degree", "constraint", "effective_size")
    .sort("constraint")
    .head(5)
)
```

The instructor and the administrator are the least constrained members, with effective sizes of
about 14 and 15: nearly all their friends are separate contacts. At the other extreme, member
`"11"` has a constraint of 1, the maximum, since their single friend is their only link to the
club. [`local_constraint()`](../reference/Graph.local_constraint.qmd) breaks a node's constraint
down by contact, and [`dispersion()`](../reference/Graph.dispersion.qmd) scores a single tie by how
poorly connected the two nodes' mutual friends are to one another, which has been used to identify
romantic partners in social networks.

## Spreaders

Some measures are designed for spreading processes, such as an epidemic or the adoption of a new
idea. [`voterank()`](../reference/Graph.voterank.qmd) picks a set of spreaders one at a time. Each
node votes for its neighbors, the node with the most votes is chosen, and then its neighbors' votes
are weakened, so that the next choice tends to lie elsewhere in the network. It returns the chosen
node IDs in order:

```{python}
karate.voterank(count=4)
```

[`percolation_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.percolation_centrality.qmd) generalizes
betweenness to a network in which each node has a *state* between 0 and 1, such as its level of
infection, and weights the paths from each source by its state. With every state equal, it reduces
to betweenness. [Spreading and robustness](spreading.qmd) covers the simulation of spreading
processes in full.

## Comparing measures

Different measures often broadly agree, and it is worth checking how far. A Spearman rank
correlation compares the orders in which two measures rank the nodes, and Polars computes it
directly from the node table:

```{python}
node_df = karate.get_node_df()
pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "measure": measures,
        **{
            other: [
                round(node_df.select(pl.corr(m, other, method="spearman")).item(), 2)
                for m in measures
            ]
            for other in ["degree_centrality", "betweenness_centrality", "pagerank"]
        },
    }
)
```

The measures are strongly correlated in the karate club, as they usually are in small, connected
social networks. Degree and PageRank are almost interchangeable here, while eigenvector centrality
agrees least with the others: it rewards a node for the company it keeps, so two members with the
same number of friends can score very differently depending on whether those friends are hubs.
When the measures disagree, the disagreement itself is informative, and it is worth looking at the
nodes responsible.

A drawing is often the quickest comparison. Sizing the nodes by betweenness and coloring them by
faction shows the two leaders, and the members between the factions, such as `"2"` and `"31"`,
who also carry much of the club's traffic:

```{python}
karate.plot(
    size_by="betweenness_centrality", color_by="faction", label_by="label", seed=4
)
```

[Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd) has more on mapping attributes to sizes and colors.

### Selecting the most central nodes

To act on the most central nodes, rather than just list them,
[`select_nodes_by_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.select_nodes_by_centrality.qmd) computes a
measure and selects the `k` highest-scoring nodes in one step. It supports `"degree"`,
`"in_degree"`, `"out_degree"`, `"pagerank"`, and `"betweenness"`, and stores no attribute. The
selection can then be passed to any `_ws` method (see [Selections](selections.qmd)), here to
tag the five members with the highest betweenness:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .select_nodes_by_centrality(measure="betweenness", k=5, set_op="replace")
    .set_node_attrs_ws(type="broker")
    .clear_selection()
    .get_node_df()
    .filter(type="broker")
    .select("id", "label", "betweenness_centrality")
)
```

`include_ties=True` selects every node tied at the cut-off, so the result may hold more than `k`
nodes.

## Performance

The measures differ greatly in cost. Degree is computed in a single pass over the edges, and the
spectral measures (eigenvector, Katz, PageRank, HITS) need a few dozen passes, so all of them are
fast on graphs with millions of edges. Closeness, harmonic, and betweenness centrality require a
shortest-path search from every node, so their cost grows with the product of the numbers of
nodes and edges. EdgeCase runs these searches in parallel in its Rust core, and computes
betweenness for the 5,000-node power grid in about half a second, but on graphs with hundreds of
thousands of nodes they become slow. The current-flow measures, which solve systems of linear
equations, are the most expensive, and are best kept to graphs of a few thousand nodes.

For large graphs, prefer the cheap measures for exploration, and use
[`approximate_current_flow_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.approximate_current_flow_betweenness_centrality.qmd)
or `prominent_group(greedy=True)` where an approximation will do.

## More measures

EdgeCase implements many more centrality measures, each designed for a particular question. They
follow the same conventions as the measures above:

| Method | Measures |
|---|---|
| [`subgraph_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph_centrality.qmd) | the closed walks through a node, with longer walks counting for less |
| [`laplacian_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.laplacian_centrality.qmd) | the drop in the graph's Laplacian energy when a node is removed |
| [`second_order_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.second_order_centrality.qmd) | the variability of a random walk's return times to a node; *lower* values are more central |
| [`closeness_vitality()`](../reference/Graph.closeness_vitality.qmd), [`node_vitality()`](../reference/Graph.node_vitality.qmd) | the increase in the total distance between all pairs when a node is removed |
| [`leverage_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.leverage_centrality.qmd) | how a node's degree compares with its neighbors' degrees |
| [`radiality()`](../reference/Graph.radiality.qmd) | how close a node is to the others, relative to the graph's diameter |
| [`bridging_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.bridging_centrality.qmd) | betweenness combined with a coefficient for lying between dense regions |
| [`domirank_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.domirank_centrality.qmd) | dominance over neighbors, from competition between nodes |
| [`knotty_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.knotty_centrality.qmd) | membership of the network's densely connected, high-betweenness core |
| [`local_reaching_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.local_reaching_centrality.qmd), [`global_reaching_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.global_reaching_centrality.qmd) | how much of a directed graph a node can reach, and how hierarchical the graph is |
| [`incremental_closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.incremental_closeness_centrality.qmd) | closeness after adding or removing a single edge, without recomputing from scratch |
| [`bipartite_degree_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_degree_centrality.qmd), [`bipartite_closeness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_closeness_centrality.qmd), [`bipartite_betweenness_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_betweenness_centrality.qmd), [`birank()`](../reference/Graph.birank.qmd) | centrality in bipartite graphs, normalized by the size of each side |

Choosing among them is a matter of matching the measure to the process of interest. If influence
travels along shortest paths, use betweenness or closeness; if it travels by every route, as rumors
and infections do, use a current-flow or spectral measure; and if only direct contact matters, use
degree. [Communities](communities.qmd) takes the next step, from important nodes to important
groups of nodes.
